--- title: "Building a Large Language Model
Part 3: GPT RLHF" author: "Jonathan Dekermanjian" date: "2026-09-06" categories: [Natural Language Processing] code-annotations: below css: styles.css jupyter: nnx_env execute: cache: true bibliography: references.bib nocite: | @* --- # Overview This is the final post in a three-part series on building a large language model from scratch. In the previous post we covered the second stage, instruction fine-tuning our pre-trained decoder-only GPT on instruction-response mappings. In this post we tackle the third stage: preference fine-tuning using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. # Introduction Training large language models (LLM)s involves training in phases where the objectives of each phase differ quite a bit. During the first phase, commonly known as pre-training, the objective is to instill the LLM with vast amounts of general knowledge. The second phase, commonly instruction tuning, molds our model that at this point carries immense general knowledge to follow instructions so that we can leverage its knowledge as an assistant on specialized tasks. This brings us to the main post-training event of this post; preference fine-tuning. Preference fine-tuning nudges the LLM to produce output responses that are aligned with some particular preference, for example, being polite. Preference training is typically acheived using reinforcement learning and the data typically consist of sets of prompts with multiple responses that are ranked by human labellers, hence the term Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). In this post we will preference tune our instruction fine-tuned model from the previous post. We will be implementing the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm, which will require us to set up the following objects: 1. A **reward model**: Stands-in for our human-judge and allows us to extend beyond just the labelled data we've collected 2. A **policy**: The instruction-tuned LLM whose weighst we are updating 3. A **reference** model: The same instruction-tuned LLM whose weights are frozen to ensure our model doesn't undergo catastrophic forgetting 4. A **critic** model: Our reward model that gets updated to accomodate a changing policy # Data Processing & Formatting As we mentioned above, instead of one "correct" response per prompt, each entry contains **two candidate responses and a judgment**: a `chosen` (preferred) response and a `rejected` one. Typically that preferrence comes from people by sampling a few responses from the SFT model, showing them to an annotator, recording the ranking. OpenAI's InstructGPT data and Anthropic's HH-RLHF dataset were both built this way. We will use the preference version of the same 1,100-example instruction dataset from the last post, published in Sebastian Raschka's [LLMs-from-scratch](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch) repository. Its `chosen`/`rejected` fields were generated synthetically, by prompting a larger model to produce a *polite* and an *impolite* paraphrase of each reference answer. ::: {#612b54a0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def download_and_load_file(file_path, url): if not os.path.exists(file_path): with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response: text_data = response.read().decode("utf-8") with open(file_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file: file.write(text_data) else: with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file: text_data = file.read() with open(file_path, "r") as file: data = json.load(file) return data file_path = "instruction-data-with-preference.json" url = ( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch" "/main/ch07/04_preference-tuning-with-dpo/instruction-data-with-preference.json" ) data = download_and_load_file(file_path, url) print("Number of entries:", len(data)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of entries: 1100 ``` ::: ::: Let's look at an enrty in our dataset ::: {#829daba0 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} entry = data[3] print("Instruction:", entry["instruction"]) print("\nChosen response:\n ", entry["chosen"]) print("\nRejected response:\n ", entry["rejected"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Instruction: Rewrite this sentence to start with 'Although': Despite the rain, they went for a walk. Chosen response: Although it was raining, they went for a walk. Rejected response: Although it was pouring buckets, they still bothered going for a walk. ``` ::: ::: ## Splitting With the data in memory, we split it into three sets: 85% for training, 10% for testing, and the remaining 5% for validation. The training set drives the weight updates, the validation set lets us monitor generalization during fine-tuning, and the held-out test set is reserved for the final qualitative evaluation. ::: {#8866ebff .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} train_portion = int(len(data) * 0.85) # 85% for training test_portion = int(len(data) * 0.1) # 10% for testing val_portion = len(data) - train_portion - test_portion # 5% for validation train_data = data[:train_portion] test_data = data[train_portion:train_portion + test_portion] val_data = data[train_portion + test_portion:] print("Training set length:", len(train_data)) print("Validation set length:", len(val_data)) print("Test set length:", len(test_data)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Training set length: 935 Validation set length: 55 Test set length: 110 ``` ::: ::: ## Formatting We reuse the same formatting as we did during instruction fine-tuning. ::: {#368140a4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def format_input(entry): instruction_text = ( f"Below is an instruction that describes a task. " f"Write a response that appropriately completes the request." f"\n\n### Instruction:\n{entry['instruction']}" ) input_text = ( f"\n\n### Input:\n{entry['input']}" if entry["input"] else "" ) return instruction_text + input_text ``` ::: ## Loading Again we load in the same tokenizer as before. ::: {#926882b8 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} tokenizer = tiktoken.get_encoding("gpt2") ``` ::: Each dataset entry becomes **two token sequences**, built exactly like our SFT sequences, one for the `chosen` response and one for the `rejected`. Two details worth mentioning: 1. **We append `<|endoftext|>` to every sequence.** The reward model will read its score at the *final* token, the only position where causal attention has seen the whole response. 2. **We keep a mask of real tokens** instead of the `-100` label trick we used in during instruction fine-tuning. We only need to know where each sequence ends so we can read the score there. As before we right-pad with `<|endoftext|>` (id 50256) to the longest sequence in the batch. Right-padding is harmless for a causal model as attention only flows left, so pad positions cannot contaminate real positions. Notice in the `collate_fn` that we pad the batch to the longest sequence across both the `chosen` and `rejected` responses. ::: {#ae0d4b6c .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} PAD_ID = EOS_ID = 50256 # <|endoftext|> plays both roles, as in the previous posts @dataclass class PreferenceDataset: """Pre-encodes every preference pair; each item holds a chosen and a rejected token sequence.""" data: list def __post_init__(self): self.encoded = [] for entry in self.data: prompt = format_input(entry) + "\n\n### Response:\n" self.encoded.append({ "chosen": tokenizer.encode(prompt + entry["chosen"]) + [EOS_ID], "rejected": tokenizer.encode(prompt + entry["rejected"]) + [EOS_ID], }) def __len__(self): return len(self.data) def __getitem__(self, idx: int): return self.encoded[idx] def preference_collate_fn(batch, pad_token_id=PAD_ID, allowed_max_length=256): longest_seq = max(max(len(item["chosen"]), len(item["rejected"])) for item in batch) batch_max_length = min( longest_seq, allowed_max_length, ) def pad_and_stack(key): ids, mask = [], [] for item in batch: seq = item[key][:allowed_max_length] ids.append(np.array(seq + [pad_token_id] * (batch_max_length - len(seq)))) mask.append(np.array([1.0] * len(seq) + [0.0] * (batch_max_length - len(seq)), dtype=np.float32)) return np.stack(ids), np.stack(mask) chosen_ids, chosen_mask = pad_and_stack("chosen") rejected_ids, rejected_mask = pad_and_stack("rejected") return chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask ``` ::: With a dataset and a collate function, we wrap everything in a `grain` data loader. ::: {#ac0cf759 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} def load_and_preprocess_data(data: list, batch_size: int, shuffle=False): dataset = PreferenceDataset(data) print(f"Loaded {len(dataset)} samples") sampler = pygrain.IndexSampler( len(dataset), shuffle=shuffle, seed=42, shard_options=pygrain.NoSharding(), num_epochs=1, ) dl = pygrain.DataLoader( data_source=dataset, sampler=sampler, operations=[ pygrain.Batch(batch_size=batch_size, drop_remainder=True, batch_fn=preference_collate_fn) ], ) return dl train_dl = load_and_preprocess_data(data=train_data, batch_size=8, shuffle=True) val_dl = load_and_preprocess_data(data=val_data, batch_size=8, shuffle=False) chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask = next(iter(train_dl)) print("chosen_ids:", chosen_ids.shape, " rejected_ids:", rejected_ids.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loaded 935 samples Loaded 55 samples chosen_ids: (8, 85) rejected_ids: (8, 85) ``` ::: ::: # Load Pretrained GPT We start preference tuning from the instruction fine-tuned model, so we need to reconstruct the architecture and load in the saved weights. The architecture is unchanged from the previous posts, with two small but important adjustments: 1. **The forward pass is split in two.**: `hidden_states()` runs everything except the output head, and `__call__` puts the language-model head on top. The reward model and the value function ("critic") will reuse the same backbone with a *different* head. 2. **Dropout is off**: This matters more than it looks: PPO compares the probability the *current* policy assigns to a token against the probability recorded when that token was *sampled*. With dropout active, those two numbers differ by random noise even before any parameter update, corrupting the importance ratios at the heart of the algorithm. ::: {#4e4cae1c .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} @dataclass class GPTConfig: vocab_size: int = 50_257 context_length: int = 256 d_model: int = 768 num_heads: int = 12 num_layers: int = 12 d_ff: int = 0 dropout_rate: float = 0.1 mha_dropout_rate: float = 0.1 def __post_init__(self): if self.d_ff == 0: self.d_ff = 4 * self.d_model def __getitem__(self, key: str): return getattr(self, key) class MultiHeadAttention(nnx.Module): """Multi-head self-attention module""" def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs): assert d_model % num_heads == 0, f"d_model ({d_model}) must be divisible by num_heads ({num_heads})" self.num_heads = num_heads self.d_model = d_model self.head_dim = d_model // num_heads self.q_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs) self.k_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs) self.v_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs) self.out_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs) self.dropout = nnx.Dropout(rate=dropout_rate, rngs=rngs) def _split_heads(self, x, batch, seq_len): return x.reshape(batch, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3) def __call__(self, x): batch, seq_len, _ = x.shape mask = jnp.triu(jnp.ones((seq_len, seq_len), dtype=bool), 1) q = self._split_heads(self.q_proj(x), batch, seq_len) k = self._split_heads(self.k_proj(x), batch, seq_len) v = self._split_heads(self.v_proj(x), batch, seq_len) attn_logits = jnp.matmul(q, k.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2)) / jnp.sqrt(self.head_dim) attn_logits = jnp.where(mask, -jnp.inf, attn_logits) attn_weights = jax.nn.softmax(attn_logits, axis=-1) attn_weights = self.dropout(attn_weights) out = jnp.matmul(attn_weights, v).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(batch, seq_len, self.d_model) return self.out_proj(out) class FeedForward(nnx.Module): """Position-wise feedforward network as used in the Transformer""" def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs): self.linear1 = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_ff, rngs=rngs) self.linear2 = nnx.Linear(d_ff, d_model, rngs=rngs) def __call__(self, x): x = self.linear1(x) x = jax.nn.gelu(x) return self.linear2(x) class TransformerBlock(nnx.Module): """Single Transformer block: multi-head self-attention followed by a feedforward network, with residual connections and layer normalization.""" def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, d_ff, mha_dropout_rate, dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs): self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, num_heads, mha_dropout_rate, rngs=rngs) self.norm1 = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs) self.ffn = FeedForward(d_model, d_ff, rngs=rngs) self.norm2 = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs) self.dropout = nnx.Dropout(rate=dropout_rate, rngs=rngs) def __call__(self, x): shortcut = x x = self.norm1(x) x = self.attention(x) x = self.dropout(x) x = x + shortcut shortcut = x x = self.norm2(x) x = self.ffn(x) x = self.dropout(x) x = x + shortcut return x class GPT(nnx.Module): def __init__(self, config: GPTConfig, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs): # Token and Position Embeddings self.token_emb = nnx.Embed(config["vocab_size"], config["d_model"], rngs=rngs) self.pos_emb = nnx.Param(jax.random.normal(rngs.params(), (1, config["context_length"], config["d_model"])) * 0.02) self.drop_emb = nnx.Dropout(rate=config["dropout_rate"], rngs=rngs) # Transformer Blocks self.blocks = nnx.List([TransformerBlock(config["d_model"], config["num_heads"], config["d_ff"], config["mha_dropout_rate"], config["dropout_rate"], rngs=rngs) for _ in range(config["num_layers"])]) self.norm_final = nnx.LayerNorm(config["d_model"], rngs=rngs) # Logits self.out_head = nnx.Linear(config["d_model"], config["vocab_size"], rngs=rngs) def hidden_states(self, input_ids): """Everything except the output head -- the seam where other heads plug in.""" _, seq_len = input_ids.shape # Combine embeddings: Token + Position x = self.token_emb(input_ids) x = x + self.pos_emb[:, :seq_len, :] x = self.drop_emb(x) for block in self.blocks: x = block(x) return self.norm_final(x) def __call__(self, input_ids): return self.out_head(self.hidden_states(input_ids)) ``` ::: # Reward Model The reward model (RM) is our stand-in for the human judge. It maps any (prompt, response) pair to a single scalar $r_\theta(x, y)$ that represents *how much would a human like this response?* Once we the model trained, the RL stage can get feedback on **any** sample the policy produces, not just the finite set of responses humans happened to label. That is the whole point of learning a reward model rather than using the preference data directly. ## Architecture The architecture of the RM will be the same as our insturction-tuned GPT, which already understands the distribution of prompts and responses it will be judging, with one adjustment. We swap the vocabulary head for a **scalar head** that gets applied at every postion where it emits a score per token. The token that we train on is the final `<|endoftext|>` token, where the model has seen the entire response. ## Loss Function Our labels are comparisons, not target scores, so we need a model of how latent scores generate observed preferences. The classic answer is the **Bradley–Terry model**, which states if the preferred response $y_w$ has latent quality $r_w$ and the rejected one $y_l$ has quality $r_l$, then $$P(y_w \succ y_l) = \sigma(r_w - r_l) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(r_w - r_l)}}$$ Maximizing the likelihood of the observed preferences under this model gives our training loss: $$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\, y_w,\, y_l)}\Big[\log \sigma\big(r_\theta(x, y_w) - r_\theta(x, y_l)\big)\Big]$$ Two properties worth noticing before we implement it: - **Only the difference of scores matters.** Adding a constant to every score leaves the loss unchanged, so the RM's absolute scale is arbitrary. This is why, during RL, we will normalize advantages rather than trust raw score magnitudes. - **We initialize the scalar head to zeros**, so every margin starts at exactly 0 and the initial loss must be exactly $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$ (the model is saying "50/50" about every pair). ::: {#00255bbf .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} class RewardModel(nnx.Module): """A GPT backbone with a scalar head instead of a vocabulary head. Returns one score per position; the meaningful one is at the sequence's final real token. The backbone keeps its (unused) vocabulary head -- a small memory tax for not having to fiddle with checkpoint structure. """ def __init__(self, backbone: GPT, d_model: int, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs): self.backbone = backbone self.reward_head = nnx.Linear(d_model, 1, kernel_init=nnx.initializers.zeros_init(), rngs=rngs) def __call__(self, input_ids): h = self.backbone.hidden_states(input_ids) return self.reward_head(h).squeeze(-1) # (batch, seq_len) ``` ::: ## Loading the Instruction Tuned Model We restore the GPT-2 medium checkpoint saved at the end of the instruction-tuning post (`GPT2_jax_sft`, 355M parameters: 24 layers, $d_{model}=1024$, 16 heads). If you followed the series with the from-scratch pretrained model instead, point `SFT_CHECKPOINT` at `GPT_jax_sft` and use the default `GPTConfig` dimensions. We will need fresh copies of these weights three times in this post (reward-model backbone, policy, reference), so we wrap the restore in a helper. Note `dropout_rate=0.0` — dropout layers hold no parameters, so the checkpoint restores into the dropout-free model without complaint. ::: {#9ecb5913 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} config = GPTConfig( vocab_size=tokenizer.n_vocab, context_length=256, d_model=1024, num_heads=16, num_layers=24, dropout_rate=0.0, # no dropout anywhere in the RLHF stage mha_dropout_rate=0.0, ) SFT_CHECKPOINT = Path("./model_checkpoint/GPT2_jax_sft") def load_sft_model(): """A fresh GPT with the instruction-tuned weights restored into it.""" model = GPT(config=config, rngs=nnx.Rngs(0)) checkpointer = orbax.PyTreeCheckpointer() restored_state = checkpointer.restore( SFT_CHECKPOINT.absolute(), args=orbax.args.PyTreeRestore(nnx.state(model)), ) nnx.update(model, restored_state) return model reward_model = RewardModel(load_sft_model(), config["d_model"], rngs=nnx.Rngs(1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /opt/miniconda3/envs/nnx_env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/orbax/checkpoint/_src/serialization/type_handlers.py:1345: UserWarning: Sharding info not provided when restoring. Populating sharding info from sharding file. Please note restoration time will be slightly increased due to reading from file. Note also that this option is unsafe when restoring on a different topology than the checkpoint was saved with. warnings.warn( ``` ::: ::: ## Training the reward model Each step pushes both members of a preference pair through the model, reads the two scores at their final tokens, and applies the Bradley–Terry loss. The margin also gives us a free metric: the fraction of pairs where the chosen response scores higher — the RM's **accuracy** — which starts at chance (50%) and should climb well above it. ::: {#91965c6d .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} def reward_at_last_token(rewards, mask): """Pick out each sequence's score at its final real token (the <|endoftext|> we appended).""" last_idx = jnp.sum(mask, axis=-1).astype(jnp.int32) - 1 return jnp.take_along_axis(rewards, last_idx[:, None], axis=1).squeeze(-1) def rm_loss_fn(model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask): r_chosen = reward_at_last_token(model(chosen_ids), chosen_mask) r_rejected = reward_at_last_token(model(rejected_ids), rejected_mask) margin = r_chosen - r_rejected loss = -jnp.mean(jax.nn.log_sigmoid(margin)) # Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood accuracy = jnp.mean((margin > 0).astype(jnp.float32)) return loss, accuracy rm_optimizer = nnx.Optimizer( reward_model, optax.adamw(learning_rate=1e-5, weight_decay=1e-1), wrt=nnx.Param, ) @nnx.jit def rm_train_step(model, optimizer, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask): (loss, accuracy), grads = nnx.value_and_grad(rm_loss_fn, has_aux=True)( model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask ) optimizer.update(model, grads) return loss, accuracy @nnx.jit def rm_eval_step(model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask): return rm_loss_fn(model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask) ``` ::: One epoch is enough. Reward models overfit quickly, they can start memorizing which surface features separated chosen from rejected in the training set rather than learning the underlying preference, and an overfit RM is dangerous downstream, because PPO will exploit any quirk it can find. ::: {#82bda8b6 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} num_epochs = 1 batch_size = 8 num_examples = len(train_data) eval_freq = 10 eval_iter = 6 rm_loss_history = [] rm_val_loss_history = [] rm_accuracy_history = [] pairs_seen_history = [] pairs_seen = 0 ema_loss = None val_ema_loss = None alpha = 0.3 for epoch in range(num_epochs): train_batch_iter = iter(train_dl) for step, batch in tqdm(enumerate(train_batch_iter), total=num_examples // batch_size): loss, accuracy = rm_train_step(reward_model, rm_optimizer, *batch) pairs_seen += batch[0].shape[0] if step > 0 and step % eval_freq == 0: loss_val = float(loss) ema_loss = loss_val if ema_loss is None else alpha * loss_val + (1 - alpha) * ema_loss rm_loss_history.append(ema_loss) rm_accuracy_history.append(float(accuracy)) pairs_seen_history.append(pairs_seen) val_losses = [ float(rm_eval_step(reward_model, *val_batch)[0]) for val_batch in itertools.islice(iter(val_dl), eval_iter) ] if val_losses: val_ema_loss = ( alpha * np.mean(val_losses) + (1 - alpha) * val_ema_loss if val_ema_loss is not None else np.mean(val_losses) ) rm_val_loss_history.append(float(val_ema_loss)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#25ec6338 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4)) axes[0].plot(pairs_seen_history, rm_loss_history, color="steelblue", linewidth=1.5, label="train loss") axes[0].plot(pairs_seen_history, rm_val_loss_history, color="orange", linewidth=2, label="validation loss") axes[0].axhline(np.log(2), color="gray", linewidth=1, linestyle="--", label="chance (ln 2)") axes[0].set_xlabel("Preference pairs seen") axes[0].set_ylabel("Bradley–Terry loss") axes[0].set_title("Reward Model Loss") axes[0].legend() axes[1].plot(pairs_seen_history, rm_accuracy_history, color="steelblue", linewidth=1.5) axes[1].axhline(0.5, color="gray", linewidth=1, linestyle="--") axes[1].set_xlabel("Preference pairs seen") axes[1].set_ylabel("Train batch accuracy") axes[1].set_title("Reward Model Accuracy") for ax in axes: ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=1142 height=374} ::: ::: ::: {#32234991 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} val_metrics = [rm_eval_step(reward_model, *batch) for batch in iter(val_dl)] val_accuracy = float(np.mean([float(accuracy) for _, accuracy in val_metrics])) print(f"Reward model validation accuracy: {val_accuracy:.1%}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reward model validation accuracy: 93.8% ``` ::: ::: Let's look at an example as a qualitative check, using an entry from our validation set. Remember the absolute values have no meaning; only the gap matters. ::: {#2fd00679 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} entry = val_data[20] prompt = format_input(entry) + "\n\n### Response:\n" print(format_input(entry), "\n") for label in ["chosen", "rejected"]: ids = jnp.asarray(tokenizer.encode(prompt + entry[label]) + [EOS_ID])[None, :] score = float(reward_model(ids)[0, -1]) print(f"{label:>8} ({score:+.2f}): {entry[label]}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Below is an instruction that describes a task. Write a response that appropriately completes the request. ### Instruction: Reverse the order of the given phrase. ### Input: sun and moon chosen (-0.26): moon and sun rejected (-1.15): Get it straight, it's moon and sun. ``` ::: ::: Let's save the weights of our trained RM ::: {#0a16cf99 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} save_directory = Path("./model_checkpoint/GPT2_jax_rm") checkpointer = orbax.PyTreeCheckpointer() checkpointer.save( save_directory.absolute(), args=orbax.args.PyTreeSave(nnx.state(reward_model)), force=True, ) del rm_optimizer # frees the Adam moments (2x model size) because we are about to load three more models ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` WARNING:absl:[process=0][thread=MainThread][operation_id=1] _SignalingThread.join() waiting for signals ([]) blocking the main thread will slow down blocking save times. This is likely due to main thread calling result() on a CommitFuture. ``` ::: ::: # Reinforcement Learning with PPO Now that we have a trained RM, generating more polite responses becomes an optimization problem. From a reinforcement learning perspective we just need to find the policy whose samples score highly. But *pure* reward maximization can produce catastropically bad results. This is because the RM is only a proxy for human judgment, trustworthy near the distribution it was trained on, an unconstrained optimizer will wander off that distribution, find inputs where the proxy is wrong, and exploit them (**reward hacking**). So RLHF actually optimizes a *regularized* objective: $$ \max_{\pi}\;\; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\; y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}\big[\, r_\theta(x, y) \,\big] \;-\; \beta\; \mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\, \pi(\cdot \mid x) \,\Vert\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x) \,\big) $$ where $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is a **frozen copy of the SFT (instruction tuned) model**. The Kullback-Leibler (KL) term is a constraint that says: earn as much reward as you can *without becoming a different model*. The coefficient $\beta$ sets the strength of the constraint. ## Language modeling as a reinforcement-learning problem To apply an RL algorithm we need to phrase generation as a Markov decision process with the following properties: - **State** $s_t$ = the prompt plus the tokens generated so far. - **Action** $a_t$ = the next token pulled from a 50,257 (vocabulary size) action space. - **Episode** = one complete response, ending at `<|endoftext|>` or a length cap. - **Reward**: the RM speaks only once, at the end of the episode. The KL constraint is applied *per token*, giving each action the reward $$r_t = -\beta \big( \log \pi(a_t \mid s_t) - \log \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a_t \mid s_t) \big) \;+\; \mathbb{1}[t = T] \; r_\theta(x, y)$$ (The per-token $\log \pi - \log \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is an unbiased single-sample estimate of the KL divergence.) ## The components of RLHF using PPO RLHF with PPO famously requires four copies of the network in memory at once. These models share identical architectures but their tasks are different. | model | role | trained? | |---|---|---| | **policy** | generates responses; the model we are improving | yes | | **reference** | frozen SFT (instruction tuned) snapshot; anchors the KL penalty | no | | **reward model** | the judge; scores finished responses | no | | **critic** | predicts the expected future reward from each prefix | yes | The critic is initialized from the trained reward model, which already knows how to read response quality. However, now it needs to learn to predict it from *partial* responses. :::{.callout-note} With GPT-2 medium this is roughly 1.4B parameters loaded in memory, before optimizer state. This is why RLHF has a reputation for being infrastructure-hungry. ::: ::: {#43ea1934 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} policy_model = load_sft_model() # the model we will train reference_model = nnx.clone(policy_model) # frozen SFT snapshot critic_model = nnx.clone(reward_model) # value function, initialized from the trained RM ``` ::: ::: {#ec841b75 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION = 8 # fresh prompts sampled per PPO iteration GROUP_SIZE = 4 # completions sampled per prompt MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 35 # response length cap NUM_ITERATIONS = 10 # 8 * 4 = 32 episodes per iteration, 320 episodes total KL_COEF = 0.1 # beta: strength of the per-token KL constraint CLIP_EPS = 0.2 # PPO clipping radius VF_COEF = 0.1 # weight of the critic's loss GAMMA = 1.0 # no discounting within a response LAM = 0.95 # GAE lambda PPO_EPOCHS = 5 # optimization passes over each rollout buffer MINIBATCH_SIZE = 8 # sequences per gradient step POLICY_LR = 1e-5 CRITIC_LR = 1e-5 # keeps every minibatch the same shape, so jit compiles the update exactly once assert (PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION * GROUP_SIZE) % MINIBATCH_SIZE == 0 ``` ::: ## Phase 1 — Rollouts: collecting experience PPO is (mostly) **on-policy**, which means that the experience it learns from must come from the current policy. Each iteration starts by *sampling* responses. Two details are easy to get wrong: - **Sample at temperature 1 with no top-k or nucleus truncation.** The math assumes the distribution we sampled from *is* the policy. Truncated sampling would make the recorded log-probabilities wrong, silently biasing every update. - **Exploration comes from sampling itself.** Greedy decoding would collect the same response every time and learn nothing new. We sample `GROUP_SIZE` completions of the **same prompt** as one batch. This is a deliberate trick: a batch of identical prompts needs no padding during generation, so our padding-mask-free model can generate correctly. (Production systems batch *different* prompts using left-padding, attention masks, and KV caches — machinery our small model doesn't need.) After generation, every rollout is right-padded to one fixed length `LMAX` so that all downstream jitted computations compile exactly once. ::: {#d5593ec4 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} train_prompts = [ np.array(tokenizer.encode(format_input(entry) + "\n\n### Response:\n")) for entry in train_data ] max_prompt_len = max(len(p) for p in train_prompts) LMAX = max_prompt_len + MAX_NEW_TOKENS assert LMAX <= config["context_length"] print(f"Longest prompt: {max_prompt_len} tokens -> every rollout padded to {LMAX} tokens") def sample_group(policy, prompt_ids, group_size, max_new_tokens, rng_key, temperature=1.0): """Sample `group_size` completions of the same prompt in one batch.""" idx = jnp.tile(jnp.asarray(prompt_ids)[None, :], (group_size, 1)) for _ in range(max_new_tokens): logits = policy(idx)[:, -1, :] / temperature rng_key, subkey = jax.random.split(rng_key) next_token = jax.random.categorical(subkey, logits, axis=-1) idx = jnp.concatenate([idx, next_token[:, None]], axis=1) return idx ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Longest prompt: 65 tokens -> every rollout padded to 100 tokens ``` ::: ::: ## Scoring a rollout For every sampled sequence, PPO needs four quantities: 1. $\log \pi(a_t \mid s_t)$ — the policy's log-probability of each response token, 2. $\log \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a_t \mid s_t)$ — the same, under the frozen reference, 3. $V(s_t)$ — the critic's value estimate at each prefix, 4. $r_\theta(x, y)$ — the reward model's score for the finished response. A convenient property of causal transformers: we don't need to record probabilities *during* the sampling loop. One forward pass over the finished sequence produces the logits at every position simultaneously — the output at position $t$ is the distribution over token $t{+}1$ — so a single pass recovers every per-token log-probability. All four quantities come from one jitted function. The **response mask** marks which of the $T{-}1$ next-token positions are actions we are training: the response tokens, up to and *including* the first `<|endoftext|>` (choosing to stop is an action too), and nothing after it. Positions outside the mask — the prompt, and padding — are excluded from every loss and every mean. ::: {#67dd1ef6 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} def token_logprobs(model, sequences): """Log-probability the model assigns to each next token: output[:, t] scores sequences[:, t+1].""" logits = model(sequences[:, :-1]) logps = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits, axis=-1) return jnp.take_along_axis(logps, sequences[:, 1:, None], axis=-1).squeeze(-1) def build_response_mask(sequences, prompt_len, eos_id=EOS_ID): """1.0 at response-token positions (in the T-1 next-token grid), up to and including the first <|endoftext|>. Must be called on the raw (unpadded) rollouts, so that padding cannot be mistaken for a generated end-of-text. """ sequences = np.asarray(sequences) responses = sequences[:, prompt_len:] is_eos = (responses == eos_id).astype(np.int64) after_first_eos = np.cumsum(is_eos, axis=1) - is_eos # > 0 strictly after the first eos response_mask = (after_first_eos == 0).astype(np.float32) mask = np.zeros((sequences.shape[0], sequences.shape[1] - 1), dtype=np.float32) mask[:, prompt_len - 1:] = response_mask return mask def pad_to_lmax(sequences, pad_id=PAD_ID): sequences = np.asarray(sequences) return np.pad(sequences, ((0, 0), (0, LMAX - sequences.shape[1])), constant_values=pad_id) @nnx.jit def score_rollouts(policy, reference, reward_model, critic, sequences, score_idx): """Everything PPO needs to know about a batch of finished rollouts, in one jitted pass.""" logprobs = token_logprobs(policy, sequences) # (batch, LMAX-1) ref_logprobs = token_logprobs(reference, sequences) # (batch, LMAX-1) values = critic(sequences[:, :-1]) # (batch, LMAX-1): V(s_t) at every prefix rm_scores = jnp.take_along_axis(reward_model(sequences), score_idx[:, None], axis=1).squeeze(-1) return logprobs, ref_logprobs, values, rm_scores ``` ::: ## From rewards to advantages A policy-gradient method increases the log-probability of each action in proportion to how good its outcome was. Using the raw return as "how good" is statistically terrible: almost every completion earns *some* reward, so every sampled token gets pushed up, just by different amounts — a very noisy signal. What we actually want to know is whether an action made things go **better than expected**. "Expected" is exactly what the **critic** provides: $V(s_t)$, an estimate of the reward that will eventually arrive if we continue from prefix $s_t$. Subtracting it centers the learning signal: the **advantage** $\hat{A}_t > 0$ means the action worked out better than the critic predicted, $< 0$ worse. This is also why a terminal-only reward still teaches *every* token: the critic redistributes the end-of-episode signal across the response, and each token is credited with how much it changed the outlook. We estimate advantages with **Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE)**. Define the one-step surprise (TD error): $$\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$$ and accumulate it backwards over the episode with a decay $\lambda$: $$\hat{A}_t = \sum_{k \ge 0} (\gamma \lambda)^k \, \delta_{t+k}$$ $\lambda$ interpolates between trusting the critic completely ($\lambda{=}0$: low variance, biased by critic errors) and trusting only observed rewards ($\lambda{=}1$: unbiased, high variance). We use the customary $\lambda{=}0.95$, and $\gamma{=}1$ — a 35-token response is a short episode; there is no reason to value late reward less. The critic itself is trained toward the **returns** $\hat{A}_t + V(s_t)$. Finally we **whiten** advantages (zero mean, unit variance) across each rollout buffer — a standard variance-reduction trick that also makes us robust to the RM's arbitrary scale. ::: {#ea297da7 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} def masked_mean(x, mask, axis=None): return jnp.sum(x * mask, axis=axis) / jnp.maximum(jnp.sum(mask, axis=axis), 1e-8) def masked_whiten(x, mask): mean = masked_mean(x, mask) var = masked_mean((x - mean) ** 2, mask) return (x - mean) * jax.lax.rsqrt(var + 1e-8) * mask def compute_gae(rewards, values, mask, gamma=GAMMA, lam=LAM): """Generalized Advantage Estimation, swept right-to-left over each response.""" batch, horizon = rewards.shape advantages = np.zeros_like(rewards) last_gae = np.zeros(batch) for t in reversed(range(horizon)): next_values = values[:, t + 1] if t < horizon - 1 else 0.0 next_mask = mask[:, t + 1] if t < horizon - 1 else 0.0 # 0 past the episode boundary delta = rewards[:, t] + gamma * next_values * next_mask - values[:, t] last_gae = delta + gamma * lam * next_mask * last_gae advantages[:, t] = last_gae advantages = advantages * mask returns = advantages + values * mask return advantages, returns ``` ::: ## The PPO objective Rollouts are expensive (all that token-by-token sampling), so we want **several gradient steps per batch** of experience. But after the first step the policy no longer matches the policy that generated the data. PPO's fix has two parts. First, an importance ratio per token corrects for the mismatch: $$\rho_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}$$ Second — the actual innovation — the ratio is **clipped**, so the objective stops rewarding movement beyond a trust region of the sampling policy: $$\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_t\Big[ \min\big( \rho_t \hat{A}_t,\;\; \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t,\, 1{-}\epsilon,\, 1{+}\epsilon)\, \hat{A}_t \big) \Big]$$ The intuition: as long as $\rho_t$ stays inside $[1{-}\epsilon,\, 1{+}\epsilon]$ this is the ordinary policy gradient. Once the policy has already moved a token's probability by more than $\epsilon$ *in the direction its advantage points*, the `min` selects the clipped branch, the objective goes flat, and that token contributes **zero gradient** — it simply drops out until the next batch of fresh rollouts. Stale data can never push the policy arbitrarily far. On our very first minibatch $\pi_\theta = \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}$, so every $\rho_t = 1$ (this is exactly why dropout had to go). The **clip fraction** — the share of tokens sitting on the clipped branch — is the standard health diagnostic: near 0 means we are barely using the trust region, while a large fraction means the policy is moving fast and the clip is doing real work. The critic is trained alongside with a mean-squared error toward the returns, and both models get global-norm gradient clipping — standard PPO hygiene. ::: {#eee226bd .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} def ppo_loss_fn(policy, critic, sequences, mask, old_logprobs, advantages, returns): logprobs = token_logprobs(policy, sequences) ratio = jnp.exp(logprobs - old_logprobs) pg_loss_unclipped = -advantages * ratio pg_loss_clipped = -advantages * jnp.clip(ratio, 1.0 - CLIP_EPS, 1.0 + CLIP_EPS) pg_loss = masked_mean(jnp.maximum(pg_loss_unclipped, pg_loss_clipped), mask) values = critic(sequences[:, :-1]) vf_loss = 0.5 * masked_mean((values - returns) ** 2, mask) loss = pg_loss + VF_COEF * vf_loss clip_fraction = masked_mean((jnp.abs(ratio - 1.0) > CLIP_EPS).astype(jnp.float32), mask) return loss, {"pg_loss": pg_loss, "vf_loss": vf_loss, "clip_fraction": clip_fraction} policy_optimizer = nnx.Optimizer( policy_model, optax.chain(optax.clip_by_global_norm(1.0), optax.adamw(POLICY_LR, weight_decay=0.0)), wrt=nnx.Param, ) critic_optimizer = nnx.Optimizer( critic_model, optax.chain(optax.clip_by_global_norm(1.0), optax.adamw(CRITIC_LR, weight_decay=0.0)), wrt=nnx.Param, ) @nnx.jit def ppo_train_step(policy, critic, policy_optimizer, critic_optimizer, sequences, mask, old_logprobs, advantages, returns): grad_fn = nnx.value_and_grad(ppo_loss_fn, argnums=(0, 1), has_aux=True) (loss, stats), (policy_grads, critic_grads) = grad_fn( policy, critic, sequences, mask, old_logprobs, advantages, returns ) policy_optimizer.update(policy, policy_grads) critic_optimizer.update(critic, critic_grads) return loss, stats ``` ::: ## The RLHF training loop Each iteration has the two phases we built above: - **Phase 1 (collect).** With parameters frozen, sample a group of completions for each of `PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION` prompts; score everything (log-probs, reference log-probs, values, RM scores); assemble per-token rewards; run GAE. - **Phase 2 (optimize).** Make `PPO_EPOCHS` shuffled minibatch passes over the buffer with the clipped objective. What to watch while it runs: - **reward** — the mean RM score of fresh samples. This is *the* number RLHF exists to increase. - **KL/token** — drift from the SFT model. It should grow slowly; if it explodes, the leash ($\beta$) is too loose or the learning rate too high. - **clip frac** — the trust region at work; expect it to hover somewhere in the 0.1–0.4 range after the first iteration. A practical note on runtime: sampling token-by-token without a KV cache dominates the cost — expect a few minutes per iteration on CPU (about an hour for the full run on an M-series machine). Set `NUM_ITERATIONS = 3` first if you just want to see the plumbing work end to end. ::: {#3739d1b4 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} sample_rng = jax.random.PRNGKey(42) shuffle_rng = np.random.default_rng(0) prompt_queue = [] reward_history = [] kl_history = [] length_history = [] clip_history = [] for iteration in range(NUM_ITERATIONS): # Phase 1: collect experience with the current policy (our trained language mode) buffer = {"sequences": [], "masks": [], "logprobs": [], "advantages": [], "returns": []} iter_scores, iter_kls, iter_lengths = [], [], [] sample_completion = None for _ in tqdm(range(PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION), desc=f"iter {iteration}: rollouts", leave=False): if not prompt_queue: prompt_queue = list(shuffle_rng.permutation(len(train_prompts))) prompt_ids = train_prompts[prompt_queue.pop()] prompt_len = len(prompt_ids) sample_rng, sample_key = jax.random.split(sample_rng) rollouts = sample_group(policy_model, prompt_ids, GROUP_SIZE, MAX_NEW_TOKENS, We compare the frozen reference (the SFT model we started from) against the RLHF-trained policy on **test prompts neither model has seen**, decoding greedily from both and scoring each response with the reward model. One honest caveat before reading the numbers: we are grading the student with the same rubric it studied — evaluating with the very reward model we optimized against inflates the result by construction (Goodhart's law again). Serious evaluations use held-out reward models and human raters. That is exactly why we also print the text: the point of choosing a politeness signal was that *you* can be the held-out judge. ::: {#0257b520 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} def generate_greedy(model, prompt_ids, max_new_tokens=MAX_NEW_TOKENS, eos_id=EOS_ID): idx = jnp.asarray(np.asarray(prompt_ids))[None, :] for _ in range(max_new_tokens): logits = model(idx)[:, -1, :] next_token = jnp.argmax(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True) if int(next_token[0, 0]) == eos_id: break idx = jnp.concatenate([idx, next_token], axis=1) return np.asarray(idx)[0] def rm_score(sequence_ids): """Score a full prompt+response, reading at an appended <|endoftext|> as in RM training.""" ids = np.concatenate([sequence_ids, [EOS_ID]]) return float(reward_model(jnp.asarray(ids)[None, :])[0, -1]) ``` ::: ::: {#3d0e6d51 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} for entry in test_data[:3]: prompt_ids = np.array(tokenizer.encode(format_input(entry) + "\n\n### Response:\n")) sft_ids = generate_greedy(reference_model, prompt_ids) rlhf_ids = generate_greedy(policy_model, prompt_ids) print("### Instruction:", entry["instruction"]) if entry["input"]: print("### Input:", entry["input"]) print(f" SFT ({rm_score(sft_ids):+.2f}):", tokenizer.decode(sft_ids[len(prompt_ids):].tolist()).strip()) print(f" RLHF ({rm_score(rlhf_ids):+.2f}):", tokenizer.decode(rlhf_ids[len(prompt_ids):].tolist()).strip()) print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ### Instruction: Rewrite the sentence using a simile. ### Input: The car is very fast. This is likely due to main thread calling result() on a CommitFuture. ``` ::: ::: # Conclusion That completes the pipeline this series set out to build: **pretraining → instruction tuning → RLHF**, all in JAX. In this final stage we 1. turned comparisons into a scalar judge via the **Bradley–Terry reward model**, 2. framed generation as an MDP and optimized *reward minus KL-to-reference* with **PPO** — four models working in concert: policy, reference, reward model, critic. ## What real systems add Everything here is the genuine algorithm, scaled down. Production RLHF adds: far more (human) preference data and episodes; adaptive KL controllers that tune $\beta$ on the fly; value-loss clipping and entropy bonuses; batched generation with left-padding, attention masks, and KV caches; and held-out reward models plus human evals to detect reward hacking — the failure mode you should be most paranoid about. If you train longer and watch the reward climb while the text degrades into obsequious boilerplate, you have witnessed Goodhart's law firsthand; that is the signal to shorten the leash. ## The landscape after PPO Classic RLHF is no longer the only game in town, and knowing it makes the alternatives easy to read: - **DPO** ([Rafailov et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)) collapses the reward model *and* the RL loop into a single supervised loss applied directly to preference pairs — a closed-form shortcut through everything we built in Parts 3 and 4. No rollouts, no critic, one model plus a frozen reference. - **GRPO** ([Shao et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300)) keeps the RL loop but drops the critic: sample a *group* of responses per prompt and use each sample's z-score within its group as the advantage. Our rollout code already samples in groups — replacing GAE with a group baseline is a lovely exercise. - **RLOO / REINFORCE variants** make a similar critic-free trade with a leave-one-out baseline. - **RLVR** replaces the learned reward model with *verifiable* rewards — unit tests, math checkers — and powers the current generation of reasoning models. ## Further reading - Christiano et al., 2017 — [Deep RL from Human Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741): the original RLHF paper. - Stiennon et al., 2020 — [Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.01325): the recipe at scale, pre-ChatGPT. - Ouyang et al., 2022 — [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155): the three-stage pipeline this series followed. - Bai et al., 2022 — [Anthropic's HH-RLHF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05862): helpfulness/harmlessness preference data at scale. - Schulman et al., 2017 — [PPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347) and Schulman et al., 2015 — [GAE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02438): the RL machinery. # References ::: {#refs} :::
